title: Tinea (ringworm) in adults
presentation: An adult with an itchy, scaly, annular rash with a raised edge and central clearing.

groups.name: Refer or escalate when
items: Diagnosis uncertain or no response to treatment

tables.title: Site and usual approach (check CKS and BNF)
rows: Skin scraping or nail clippings for mycology; oral antifungal is usually needed
Avoid topical steroid alone; it can mask the rash (tinea incognito)

investigations.test: Skin scrapings, nail clippings or hair for mycology
investigations.why: Confirm before oral treatment, and when the diagnosis is unclear, widespread or nail or scalp disease

investigations.test: Consider LFTs or drug review before oral antifungals

management: Topical antifungal for localised disease; continue after the rash clears (check CKS for duration).
Treat the feet as well as the groin if both are affected.
Hygiene: do not share towels, dry skin folds, change socks, wash clothing and bedding hot.
Identify and treat the source, including pets.
Safety-netting: review if no improvement in 2 weeks, or if spreading, painful, weeping or with fever.
redFlags: Immunosuppression or diabetes with extensive or recurrent disease
Failure to respond: reconsider the diagnosis
pearls: Annular scaly rash with an active edge and central clearing = think tinea, but scrape if unsure.
Ask about pets and contacts as well as treatment history.
lookUp: NICE CKS thresholds for oral treatment and mycology
Which topical agents are first line locally (BNF and formulary)
Recurrent tinea and underlying diabetes screening

selfTest.q: Why avoid hydrocortisone alone on a suspected tinea?
selfTest.a: It suppresses inflammation and alters the appearance (tinea incognito) while the fungus persists.

selfTest.q: When should you take samples for mycology?
selfTest.a: Before oral therapy, for nail or scalp disease, extensive disease, or an uncertain diagnosis.
